Q128910.title: All lines lead to him
Q128910.story: Every line of the ceiling and walls points to Jesus's head, so your eye always returns to him. Restorers found a tiny hole at that exact spot, left by a nail Leonardo used to guide his perspective lines with string.

Q128910.title: Judas in the shadows
Q128910.story: Judas leans back from the table, clutching a small bag, often read as the silver he was paid. He is the only apostle whose face falls into shadow.

Q128910.title: Peter's knife
Q128910.story: Behind Judas, Peter leans forward with a knife in his hand. It hints at what comes later that night, when Peter draws a blade in the garden.

Q128910.title: A halo made of daylight
Q128910.story: Leonardo painted no golden halo around Jesus. Instead, the bright window behind him frames his head with light, doing the same job in a more natural way.

Q128910.title: The missing feet
Q128910.story: In 1652, the monks cut a doorway into the wall below the painting, slicing away Jesus's feet. Leonardo had also experimented with painting on dry plaster, which is why the mural began flaking within his own lifetime.

Q474338.title: Not quite a pet
Q474338.story: The white animal is an ermine, a symbol of purity. It is also a clever pun: the Greek word for ermine sounds like the sitter's surname, Gallerani, and her powerful patron Ludovico Sforza was nicknamed 'the ermine'.

Q474338.title: Caught mid-turn
Q474338.story: Instead of posing stiffly, Cecilia twists to look at someone outside the picture. Portraits of the time were usually flat profiles, so this sense of a living moment was strikingly new.

Q474338.title: Leonardo's study of hands
Q474338.story: Look at her long, bony fingers resting on the ermine. Leonardo, who dissected bodies to understand anatomy, painted every knuckle and tendon with care.

Q1892745.title: The puzzling orb
Q1892745.story: Christ holds a clear crystal orb. Some critics point out that real solid glass would bend and distort what's behind it, yet here it barely does, a puzzle in a painting whose attribution experts still debate.

Q1892745.title: The most expensive painting ever sold
Q1892745.story: In 2017 this painting sold at auction for about 450 million US dollars, the highest price ever paid for a painting. Its whereabouts since then have been the subject of much speculation.

Q1217213.title: Wings that grew
Q1217213.story: The angel Gabriel's wings were based on real birds' wings. A later painter lengthened them, and you can still see the extended part painted over the landscape.

Q1217213.title: A borrowed design
Q1217213.story: Mary's reading stand is carved like a tomb made by Leonardo's teacher, Verrocchio. This is one of Leonardo's earliest works, painted while he was still training in Verrocchio's workshop.

Q500242.title: The almost-touch
Q500242.story: The two fingers don't quite meet. That tiny gap is the moment just before life passes from God to Adam, and it has become one of the most copied details in all of art.

Q500242.title: Waiting for life
Q500242.story: Adam lies relaxed, his arm hanging limply, as if he has a body but not yet the spark of life. Compare it with the powerful, rushing figure of God.

Q500242.title: A hidden brain?
Q500242.story: In 1990 a doctor noticed that the red cloak around God and the angels is shaped remarkably like a human brain. Some think Michelangelo, who studied anatomy, did this on purpose; others think it is a coincidence.

Q500242.title: Who is under God's arm?
Q500242.story: A woman peers out from under God's arm. She is often identified as Eve, not yet created, waiting her turn.

Q567861.title: The judge at the centre
Q567861.story: Christ raises his arm at the centre of a huge swirl of more than three hundred figures, deciding who rises to heaven and who falls. Michelangelo painted it on the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel, decades after the ceiling.

Q567861.title: Michelangelo's hidden self-portrait
Q567861.story: Saint Bartholomew holds up a flayed human skin, the way he was martyred. The sagging face on the skin is widely believed to be Michelangelo's own self-portrait.

Q567861.title: Revenge with donkey ears
Q567861.story: In the bottom corner stands Minos, judge of the underworld, with donkey ears and a snake wrapped around him. His face is said to belong to a papal official who complained about all the nudity, Michelangelo's way of getting even.

Q567861.title: The added clothes
Q567861.story: After Michelangelo died, church authorities ordered many nude figures covered. The painter who added the cloths and loincloths was mockingly nicknamed 'the breeches maker'.

Q1473546.title: A rare finished panel
Q1473546.story: This round painting of the Holy Family is the only finished panel painting firmly accepted as Michelangelo's. He thought of himself as a sculptor first, and the twisting, muscular figures look almost carved.

Q1473546.title: Strangers in the background
Q1473546.story: Behind the family lounge several nude young men. Their meaning is still debated; one common idea is that they stand for the ancient world before Christianity.

Q186953.title: Up versus down
Q186953.story: At the centre walk Plato and Aristotle. Plato points upward to the world of ideas, while Aristotle holds his hand flat over the earth, summing up their two philosophies in a single gesture. Plato is traditionally said to have Leonardo da Vinci's face.

Q186953.title: The brooding thinker
Q186953.story: The figure leaning on a block of marble, lost in thought, is usually identified as Heraclitus. He seems to have been added after the rest was painted, and many believe he is a portrait of Michelangelo, who was working on the Sistine ceiling nearby.

Q186953.title: Geometry lesson
Q186953.story: Bending over a slate with a compass, a mathematician, usually called Euclid or Archimedes, shows students a diagram. He is thought to be modelled on Raphael's friend, the architect Bramante.

Q186953.title: Raphael looks back at you
Q186953.story: Near the right edge, a young man in a dark cap gazes straight out of the picture. This is Raphael himself, slipping his self-portrait in among the great minds.

Q328079.title: The famous little angels
Q328079.story: Two bored-looking cherubs lean on the ledge at the bottom. They have become far more famous than the painting around them, appearing on everything from postcards to umbrellas.

Q328079.title: Pointing at you
Q328079.story: Pope Sixtus II points out of the painting toward the viewer, while his papal crown rests on the ledge. It is as if he is presenting Mary and the child to the people in the church.

Q2344505.title: A bird with a message
Q2344505.story: The two children play with a goldfinch, the painting's namesake. Goldfinches eat thistle seeds, and thistles recalled Christ's crown of thorns, so the cheerful bird quietly foretells his suffering.

Q2344505.title: Pieced back together
Q2344505.story: In 1547 the house where this painting hung collapsed, and the panel broke into many pieces. It was repaired, and a careful modern restoration finished in 2008 revealed its colours again.

Q151047.title: A goddess born from the sea
Q151047.story: Venus arrives on the shore fully grown, standing in a pose borrowed from ancient Roman statues of the modest Venus. Look closely and her neck is unusually long and her shoulder slopes impossibly, yet she still seems perfectly balanced.

Q151047.title: Blown ashore
Q151047.story: On the left, the wind god Zephyr and a companion blow Venus toward land, while roses tumble through the air around them.

Q151047.title: A cloak of flowers
Q151047.story: On the right, a goddess of the seasons rushes forward with a flowered cloak, ready to cover Venus as she steps onto land.

Q151047.title: The scallop shell
Q151047.story: Venus rides a giant scallop shell across the waves. The painting was made on canvas rather than wood, unusual in Florence at the time for such a large work.

Q549847.title: Love is blind
Q549847.story: Above Venus hovers a blindfolded Cupid, aiming a flaming arrow at the dancing women below. Love, the painting suggests, strikes without looking.

Q549847.title: The Three Graces
Q549847.story: Three women in transparent gowns dance in a circle, their hands linked. They are the Graces, ancient symbols of beauty, charm and joy.

Q549847.title: A chase becomes spring
Q549847.story: On the right, the blue wind Zephyr catches the nymph Chloris. Flowers spill from her mouth as she transforms into Flora, the goddess of spring, who strides beside her in a flowered dress.

Q549847.title: A garden of real plants
Q549847.story: Botanists have identified around 500 plants in this painting, including about 190 different flowers, many of them blooming around Florence in springtime.

Q2293953.title: A buzzing pun
Q2293953.story: Wasps swarm around a nest near Mars's head. The Italian for wasp is 'vespa', which may be a playful nod to the Vespucci family, who were connected with Botticelli.

Q2293953.title: Mischief-makers
Q2293953.story: While Mars sleeps after love, little satyrs play with his armour and lance, one even blowing a shell into his ear. Love has disarmed war.

Q969377.title: A beam of light
Q969377.story: A sharp beam of light cuts across the dark room, following the direction of Christ's pointing hand, as if the call itself were made of light.

Q969377.title: A famous hand
Q969377.story: Christ's outstretched hand closely echoes Adam's hand in Michelangelo's Creation of Adam, a deliberate link to another moment of being called into new life.

Q969377.title: Which one is Matthew?
Q969377.story: The bearded man seems to point at himself, asking 'Me?' Yet some art historians argue Matthew is actually the young man at the end of the table, still counting his coins. The debate continues.

Q2470123.title: Reluctant courage
Q2470123.story: Judith frowns as she does the deed, half determined and half disgusted. Caravaggio was famous for showing violent stories with startling realism.

Q2470123.title: The old servant
Q2470123.story: Beside her, the wrinkled old maid clutches a bag for the head, her face tense with eager concentration. Her age makes Judith look even younger.

Q2293905.title: The painter as monster
Q2293905.story: Medusa screams at the moment her head is cut off. Many believe Caravaggio used his own face for her.

Q2293905.title: Painted on a shield
Q2293905.story: This painting is on a real, curved ceremonial shield, made as a gift for the Grand Duke of Tuscany. The curve makes the snakes seem to writhe outward toward you.

Q318947.title: About to fall
Q318947.story: The fruit basket teeters on the very edge of the table, its shadow falling toward you. It seems ready to tumble out of the painting into your space.

Q318947.title: An unexpected face
Q318947.story: Christ is shown young and beardless, which surprised viewers used to bearded images of him. It fits the story: the disciples did not recognise him at first.

Q219831.title: The captain's command
Q219831.story: Captain Frans Banninck Cocq, in black with a red sash, gives the order to march. His outstretched hand casts a shadow onto his lieutenant's bright yellow coat.

Q219831.title: The mysterious girl in gold
Q219831.story: A glowing girl moves through the crowd with a dead chicken hanging from her belt. Its claws were the symbol of this militia company, so she works like a living mascot.

Q219831.title: Not actually night
Q219831.story: This is a daytime scene. Layers of old varnish darkened it so much that it gained the nickname The Night Watch, long after Rembrandt's death.

Q219831.title: Cut to fit
Q219831.story: In 1715, the painting was moved to Amsterdam's town hall and trimmed on all sides to fit between two doors. Strips were lost, including two figures on the left.

Q661378.title: Starting with the arm
Q661378.story: Dr Tulp lifts the muscles of the forearm with forceps. Real dissections usually began with the stomach, so beginning with the arm let Rembrandt show the hand, a symbol of human skill.

Q661378.title: The famous doctor
Q661378.story: Dr Nicolaes Tulp was a leading Amsterdam surgeon. This group portrait, paid for by the surgeons in it, made young Rembrandt's reputation.

Q661378.title: The man on the table
Q661378.story: The body belongs to Aris Kindt, a criminal hanged for armed robbery earlier that day. Public dissections were allowed only on executed criminals.

Q2246489.title: Rembrandt on board
Q2246489.story: Among the terrified disciples, one man clutches his cap and looks straight out at you. He is thought to be Rembrandt himself.

Q2246489.title: A painting still missing
Q2246489.story: This is Rembrandt's only known seascape, and nobody has seen it since 1990, when thieves stole it from the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston. Its empty frame still hangs there, waiting.

Q167605.title: A thin stream of milk
Q167605.story: The milk pours in a fine, steady stream, a calm, frozen moment of everyday work. The whole painting feels unusually still and quiet.

Q167605.title: Sparkling bread
Q167605.story: The bread and basket are covered in tiny dots of bright paint. Vermeer used these points of light to make crusts and wicker seem to glitter.

Q167605.title: The foot warmer
Q167605.story: On the floor sits a small foot warmer, a box for hot coals, beside Delft tiles decorated with a little Cupid. Scholars still debate whether Cupid hints at the maid's private thoughts.

Q167605.title: The bare wall
Q167605.story: Look at the white wall: you can spot a nail and the hole where another one used to be. X-rays show Vermeer originally painted something hanging there, then painted over it to keep the wall simple.

Q523974.title: A little patch of yellow wall
Q523974.story: The French novelist Marcel Proust adored this painting and wrote about a small patch of sunlit yellow wall in it, calling the work one of the most beautiful paintings in the world.

Q523974.title: Sun on the New Church
Q523974.story: Clouds shade the foreground, while sunlight falls on the town behind, catching the tower of the New Church. The play of shadow and light makes the city glow.

Q588695.title: The painter's back
Q588695.story: The artist sits with his back to us, so we never see his face. Some believe it is Vermeer himself, but we cannot be sure.

Q588695.title: The muse of history
Q588695.story: The model holds a trumpet and a book and wears a laurel crown, dressed as Clio, the muse of history. The painter is turning an ordinary girl into an idea.

Q588695.title: An out-of-date map
Q588695.story: The large wall map shows the Netherlands before it split into a northern and southern part, a world that no longer existed by Vermeer's time. A crease runs down its middle like the divide itself.

Q7487097.title: A clever excuse
Q7487097.story: Shakuntala pretends to pull a thorn from her foot, but she is really looking back at King Dushyanta, with whom she has fallen in love. The scene comes from Kalidasa's famous Sanskrit play.

Q7487097.title: Art for every home
Q7487097.story: Raja Ravi Varma set up a printing press, and cheap prints of paintings like this spread across India. For many families, these were the first artworks they ever owned.

Q55373382.title: A family moment
Q55373382.story: The woman and child are believed to be modelled on the painter's own daughter and grandson, eagerly turning as father returns home.

Q55373282.title: Women from across India
Q55373282.story: Each musician wears the dress of a different region of India, from Kerala to Kashmir. Ravi Varma brought them together to show the country's variety in a single scene.

Q154469.title: Hands that dug the earth
Q154469.story: Van Gogh wrote that he wanted to show these peasants eating potatoes with the very hands they used to dig the soil. Their rough, bony hands are the heart of the picture.

Q154469.title: A single lamp
Q154469.story: One small lamp lights the whole room, casting deep shadows. Van Gogh considered this dark early work one of his most important paintings.

Q1025704.title: A night sky without black
Q1025704.story: This was the first painting in which Van Gogh used a starry sky. He wrote proudly that he had painted the night without using any black, only deep blues, violets and greens.

Q1025704.title: Painted on the spot
Q1025704.story: Van Gogh set up his easel in the street in Arles and painted this café at night, by the light of the gas lamp glowing under the yellow awning.

Q634122.title: Not his last painting
Q634122.story: Legend says this was Van Gogh's final painting before his death, but letters and research suggest he made other works after it.

Q634122.title: Roads to nowhere
Q634122.story: Three paths cut through the wheat, but none seems to lead anywhere, while crows scatter across a stormy sky.

Q2282256.title: Painted in the asylum garden
Q2282256.story: Van Gogh painted these irises in the garden of the asylum at Saint-Rémy, in his first week there. In 1987 it sold for a record-breaking price at the time.

Q328523.title: A sun that vanishes
Q328523.story: The orange sun seems to blaze, but it is almost exactly as bright as the grey sky around it. Turn the painting black and white and the sun nearly disappears.

Q328523.title: The painting that named a movement
Q328523.story: A critic mocked this painting's title, Impression, calling the whole group of artists 'Impressionists'. The insult stuck, and became the name of one of art's most loved movements.

Q328523.title: Quick strokes
Q328523.story: The little rowing boats are made of just a few dabs of dark paint. Monet painted the port of Le Havre fast, trying to catch a fleeting morning moment.

Q2395218.title: Camille in the wind
Q2395218.story: Monet's wife Camille stands on a hill, her veil and dress caught by the breeze. He painted from below, so she seems to stand against the open sky.

Q2395218.title: Their son Jean
Q2395218.story: Further back stands the couple's young son Jean, half hidden by the grass.

Q1167912.title: A painting in pieces
Q1167912.story: Monet planned a huge picnic scene but couldn't pay his rent, and left the canvas with his landlord. When he got it back, it was damaged by damp, so he cut it up. Only fragments survive.

Q683274.title: Dappled sunlight
Q683274.story: Spots of sunlight filter through the trees onto jackets and dresses. Renoir captured how light dances over a crowd on a Sunday afternoon in Montmartre.

Q683274.title: A party of friends
Q683274.story: Many of the dancers and chatting figures were Renoir's own friends, which gives the scene its relaxed, happy feeling.

Q1167907.title: The woman with the dog
Q1167907.story: The young woman playing with a little dog is Aline Charigot, a seamstress who later married Renoir.

Q1167907.title: The painter on the chair
Q1167907.story: The man sitting backwards on his chair is the painter Gustave Caillebotte, a friend of Renoir and an important supporter of the Impressionists.

Q1239950.title: The green drink
Q1239950.story: In front of the woman sits a glass of absinthe, a strong green spirit popular in Paris cafés. Critics found the painting shocking.

Q1239950.title: Not really drinkers
Q1239950.story: The two figures were posed by Degas's friends, the actress Ellen Andrée and the painter Marcel Desboutin. Many viewers assumed they were real drunkards, which annoyed them.

Q2734209.title: A real tutu
Q2734209.story: This dancer is a sculpture, and Degas dressed her in a real fabric tutu and a silk ribbon in her hair. When first shown, many found it shockingly lifelike.

Q3821820.title: The ballet master
Q3821820.story: At the centre, leaning on a stick, stands Jules Perrot, a famous dancer and ballet master, watching his students closely.

Q3956440.title: A table that doesn't line up
Q3956440.story: The front edge of the table is not straight: the left and right parts sit at different heights. Cézanne bent the rules of perspective to show objects from several viewpoints at once.

Q3956440.title: The tilting bottle
Q3956440.story: The bottle leans as if it's about to tip over. This freedom with shape inspired later artists, including Picasso and the Cubists.

Q3210778.title: His favourite mountain
Q3210778.story: Cézanne painted Mont Sainte-Victoire, near his home in Provence, dozens of times. Each version breaks the landscape into patches of colour a little more.

Q698487.title: Real gold leaf
Q698487.story: Klimt used real gold leaf in this painting, inspired by the glittering gold mosaics he admired in churches in Ravenna, Italy.

Q698487.title: Squares for him
Q698487.story: The man's robe is covered in black, white and gold rectangles, hard-edged and upright.

Q698487.title: Circles for her
Q698487.story: The woman's dress is filled with circles and flowers. The two patterns melt together as the lovers embrace.

Q698487.title: On the edge
Q698487.story: The couple kneel at the very edge of a flower meadow, and her toes curl over the drop. Their perfect moment seems to hang right above an abyss.

Q354396.title: Adele Bloch-Bauer
Q354396.story: Adele was a Viennese hostess whose husband, a sugar industrialist, commissioned this portrait. Klimt worked on it for about three years.

Q354396.title: Eyes in the dress
Q354396.story: Look closely at her golden dress: it is scattered with eye-shaped symbols, inspired by ancient Egyptian art.

Q354396.title: Stolen and returned
Q354396.story: The Nazis seized this painting from Adele's family. Decades later, her niece Maria Altmann won a long legal battle to get it back, a story told in the film Woman in Gold.

Q2324643.title: The head at the edge
Q2324643.story: At the bottom edge, half cut off, is the head of Holofernes. Klimt pushes it almost out of the painting, so all attention falls on Judith's face.

Q2324643.title: The golden choker
Q2324643.story: A wide gold choker wraps Judith's neck, seeming to separate her head from her body, an eerie echo of what has just happened to Holofernes.

Q1683743.title: Love or vampire?
Q1683743.story: Munch first called this painting Love and Pain. A writer friend described it as a vampire biting its victim, and that title stuck, even though it may simply show a tender embrace.

Q18208623.title: The Scream's sky again
Q18208623.story: The blood-red sky and the curving fjord also appear in Munch's famous The Scream. Here, a whole crowd of pale, staring faces shares that same anxious mood.

Q252485.title: Tiny Mount Fuji
Q252485.story: Japan's sacred Mount Fuji, usually towering and grand, looks tiny here, like just another wave. The giant wave seems ready to swallow even the mountain.

Q252485.title: Claws of foam
Q252485.story: The foam at the wave's crest breaks into finger-like claws reaching for the boats. It is one of the most recognisable shapes in all of art.

Q252485.title: Rowers holding on
Q252485.story: Three fishing boats carry rowers who duck their heads as the wave rises over them. These fast boats rushed fresh fish to the markets of Edo, today's Tokyo.

Q252485.title: A new blue
Q252485.story: Hokusai used Prussian blue, a pigment imported from Europe that was new and exciting in Japan. This print is a woodblock print, so thousands of copies were made.

Q3565037.title: Red Fuji
Q3565037.story: This print is nicknamed Red Fuji. In late summer or early autumn, the morning sun can turn the mountain's slopes red for a few moments.

Q3565037.title: Rows of clouds
Q3565037.story: Small white clouds line up in the blue sky like fish scales, adding a gentle rhythm above the mountain.

Q18173384.title: Storm below, calm above
Q18173384.story: Lightning flashes across the dark lower slopes, while the summit stands above the storm in clear sky.

Q1245354.title: The barmaid's faraway look
Q1245354.story: The barmaid was a real worker at the Folies-Bergère, a lively Paris music hall, who posed for Manet in his studio. Amid all the noise and glitter, she looks tired and lost in thought.

Q1245354.title: A mirror that doesn't add up
Q1245354.story: Everything behind her is a reflection in a huge mirror. But her reflection is shifted far to the right, and the man in the top hat should be blocking our view. Manet broke the rules of reflection on purpose, and people still argue about why.

Q1245354.title: Feet in the corner
Q1245354.story: In the top left corner dangle two small green shoes. They belong to a trapeze artist performing high above the crowd, almost cut out of the picture.

Q1245354.title: Real brands on the bar
Q1245354.story: Look at the beer bottles with a red triangle on the label: that is the logo of Bass, a real English beer. It was one of Manet's last major paintings.

Q1452762.title: Split in two
Q1452762.story: A tall lamppost cuts the painting in half, separating the couple walking toward us from the open, rainy square behind them.

Q1452762.title: A brand-new Paris
Q1452762.story: The wide streets and identical stone buildings were brand new, part of a huge rebuilding of Paris in the 1850s and 1860s. Caillebotte painted the modern city as it was being born.

Q1766454.title: Too ordinary for the Salon
Q1766454.story: Three shirtless men scrape a wooden floor. The official Paris Salon rejected the painting in 1875, finding working men an unworthy subject, so Caillebotte showed it with the Impressionists instead.

Q2339059.title: Speed out of the mist
Q2339059.story: A steam train rushes toward us across a bridge over the River Thames. Turner painted it in 1844, when train travel still felt thrilling and new.

Q2339059.title: The hidden hare
Q2339059.story: Look carefully on the tracks ahead of the train: a small hare is running for its life. Some see it as nature trying to outrun the new machine age.

Q2339059.title: The old way of travel
Q2339059.story: On the river below, a small boat drifts slowly, a quiet contrast to the roaring speed above.

Q500951.title: A yellow crucifix
Q500951.story: The yellow figure of Christ was inspired by a wooden crucifix in a small chapel near Pont-Aven in Brittany, where Gauguin was working.

Q500951.title: Breton women
Q500951.story: Local women in traditional Breton dress sit around the cross. Gauguin used flat areas of strong colour instead of realistic shading, a big step away from Impressionism.

Q1044742.title: Made of dots
Q1044742.story: The whole painting is built from tiny dots of pure colour, a method called pointillism. Up close you see dots; step back and your eye mixes them into colours. It took Seurat about two years.

Q1044742.title: A monkey on a leash
Q1044742.story: The fashionable woman on the right walks a pet monkey on a leash. Exotic pets were a trendy status symbol in 1880s Paris.

Q1044742.title: Fishing on Sunday
Q1044742.story: On the left, a woman is fishing at the water's edge. Some historians see a pun here, since the French words for 'to fish' and 'to sin' sound almost the same.

Q1044742.title: A painted frame
Q1044742.story: Look at the edges: Seurat later added a border of dots in darker colours, so the painting has its own built-in frame.

Q890678.title: Reading right to left
Q890678.story: Gauguin meant this huge painting to be read from right to left, like a life story: it begins with a sleeping baby on the right.

Q890678.title: The end of life
Q890678.story: On the far left, an old woman crouches in thought, near the end of her life. Between the baby and her, figures reach, pick fruit and wonder.

Q890678.title: The question in the corner
Q890678.story: Gauguin wrote the painting's title in French in the top left corner. He painted it in Tahiti and considered it his greatest work.

Q1219263.title: A curious lion
Q1219263.story: A lion sniffs at a sleeping traveller under the moonlight, yet does not attack. The scene feels calm and dreamlike rather than dangerous.

Q1219263.title: A self-taught painter
Q1219263.story: Henri Rousseau worked as a customs official and taught himself to paint. Critics mocked his simple style, but later artists, including Picasso, admired him.

Q3869871.title: A record-breaking sale
Q3869871.story: In 2015 this painting was reportedly sold privately for around 210 million US dollars, among the highest prices ever paid for a work of art.

Q960447.title: A jungle in Paris
Q960447.story: Rousseau never travelled outside France. He imagined his jungles from visits to the botanical gardens and zoo in Paris, and from pictures in books.

Q18210019.title: Three famous faces
Q18210019.story: These were three real women, celebrated beauties of the city of Edo, today's Tokyo. Prints like this worked a bit like posters of celebrities today.

Q5826309.title: Lines of rain
Q5826309.story: Hiroshige shows the downpour with fine dark lines slicing across the sky, while people hurry over the bridge under hats and umbrellas.

Q5826309.title: Copied by Van Gogh
Q5826309.story: Van Gogh loved Japanese prints so much that he painted his own copy of this one in oil, adding a colourful border with Japanese characters.

Q766782.title: A tender gesture
Q766782.story: The man gently rests his hand on the woman's chest, and she touches his hand with her fingers. The gesture is affectionate and protective. Nobody knows for sure who the couple were.

Q766782.title: Paint like sculpture
Q766782.story: Rembrandt built up the golden sleeve with very thick paint, almost like carving it. Van Gogh said he would give years of his life to sit in front of this painting for two weeks with only a crust of bread.

Q586035.title: The street that was found
Q586035.story: For centuries nobody knew exactly where this little street was. In 2015 a researcher used old tax records to identify the spot in Delft, where Vermeer's aunt had lived.

Q969367.title: Empty scales
Q969367.story: The woman holds a delicate balance, but look closely: its pans are empty. She is not weighing treasure, only waiting for the scale to settle.

Q969367.title: A painting behind her
Q969367.story: On the wall behind hangs a painting of the Last Judgment, when souls are weighed. It quietly echoes the balance in her hand.

Q700251.title: The Cupid that came back
Q700251.story: For centuries the wall behind the girl was blank. A restoration completed in 2021 removed paint added by someone else after Vermeer's death, revealing a large picture of Cupid hanging on the wall.

Q700251.title: Her face in the window
Q700251.story: Look at the open window: the glass reflects the girl's face as she reads her letter.

Q311243.title: A figure seen from behind
Q311243.story: The man stands with his back to us, so we look out over the fog with him. This pose became one of the great symbols of the Romantic movement.

Q311243.title: A made-up view
Q311243.story: Friedrich combined sketches of real rocks and peaks in the mountains near Dresden to create this view. No single place looks exactly like it.

Q2366825.title: The hay wain
Q2366825.story: A wain is a horse-drawn farm cart. Here it splashes through a shallow river, cooling the horses' hooves and the wooden wheels.

Q2366825.title: A real cottage
Q2366825.story: The cottage on the left belonged to a farmer called Willy Lott, and it still stands today in Suffolk, England, near the mill where Constable's father worked.

Q2366825.title: A hit in Paris
Q2366825.story: When this painting was shown in Paris in 1824 it won a gold medal, and its fresh, natural skies inspired a generation of French painters.

Q2666439.title: A painting with two painters
Q2666439.story: Shishkin painted the forest, but the bear cubs were painted by his friend Konstantin Savitsky. The collector Pavel Tretyakov later removed Savitsky's signature, so the work became known as Shishkin's alone.

Q2666439.title: On a famous sweet wrapper
Q2666439.story: In Russia this picture became hugely popular as the image on the wrapper of a well-loved chocolate sweet.

Q257580.title: A ghostly warship
Q257580.story: The pale ship is the Temeraire, which fought at the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805. Here it is being towed away to be broken up for scrap, looking almost like a ghost.

Q257580.title: The new age
Q257580.story: A small, dark steam tug pulls the grand old sailing ship. Many see it as the new age of steam replacing the age of sail.

Q257580.title: Britain's favourite painting
Q257580.story: A blazing sunset seems to say goodbye to the old ship. In 2005 a public vote named this Britain's greatest painting, and it appears on the British twenty-pound note.

Q219344.title: A protest in paint
Q219344.story: This painting is based on a terrible real practice: captains of slave ships throwing enslaved people overboard. Turner showed it in 1840, as campaigners worked to end slavery around the world.

Q194137.title: A ship crushed by ice
Q194137.story: Half hidden among the jagged slabs of ice lies a wrecked ship. Friedrich was inspired by reports of Arctic expeditions trapped in frozen seas.

Q18683017.title: A meeting that never happened
Q18683017.story: Emperor Jahangir embraces Shah Abbas of Persia, but the two rulers never actually met. The painting is a dream of power, showing Jahangir as the larger, greater ruler.

Q18683017.title: Standing on the world
Q18683017.story: The rulers stand on a globe, Jahangir on a lion and Shah Abbas on a lamb, a clear message about who held the real strength.

Q22946905.title: Part of a giant storybook
Q22946905.story: This painting comes from the Hamzanama, a huge illustrated adventure story ordered by Emperor Akbar. It once contained around 1,400 large paintings, made by many artists over about fifteen years.

Q321303.title: Paradise on the left
Q321303.story: The left panel shows the Garden of Eden, with God introducing Adam to Eve. Even here, Bosch slips in strange creatures, hinting at trouble to come.

Q321303.title: A garden of giant fruit
Q321303.story: In the centre panel, crowds of people play among giant strawberries, birds and shells. Nobody agrees what it all means, which is part of its fascination five hundred years later.

Q321303.title: The tree-man
Q321303.story: In the dark right panel, a strange figure with a hollow eggshell body and tree-trunk legs looks back over his shoulder. Some believe his face is a self-portrait of Bosch.

Q220859.title: A mirror that shows more
Q220859.story: The round mirror on the back wall reflects the couple from behind, plus two more people standing in the doorway, where we would be. One of them may be the painter himself.

Q220859.title: Jan van Eyck was here
Q220859.story: Above the mirror, in fancy lettering, van Eyck wrote in Latin 'Jan van Eyck was here, 1434', more like a witness's signature than an artist's.

Q220859.title: The little dog
Q220859.story: A small dog stands at the couple's feet. Dogs often symbolised loyalty, and this one is painted hair by hair.

Q220859.title: One candle burning
Q220859.story: In the brass chandelier, only one candle is lit, even though it is daytime. Its meaning is still debated.

Q734834.title: The mystic lamb
Q734834.story: In the lower centre, crowds gather around a lamb on an altar, a symbol of Christ. A recent restoration revealed the lamb's original, surprisingly human-looking face, which had been painted over centuries ago.

Q734834.title: The panel still missing
Q734834.story: The lower left panel, called the Just Judges, was stolen in 1934 and has never been found. What you see there is a copy.

Q734834.title: The most stolen artwork?
Q734834.story: This altarpiece has been looted, sold, hidden and recovered many times. During the Second World War, the Nazis took it and stored it in a salt mine in Austria, where Allied forces recovered it in 1945.

Q546297.title: Seen from the feet
Q546297.story: Mantegna painted Christ's body from a dramatic low angle, feet first, squeezing a whole body into a short space. This bold trick is called foreshortening.

Q1267893.title: A plant that spells her name
Q1267893.story: Behind Ginevra grows a spiky juniper bush. The Italian word for juniper, 'ginepro', sounds like her name, a clever visual pun.

Q1267893.title: Leonardo in America
Q1267893.story: This is the only painting by Leonardo da Vinci on public display in the Americas, at the National Gallery of Art in Washington.

Q500985.title: A poor day's hunting
Q500985.story: Tired hunters trudge home through the snow with their dogs, carrying just one small fox. It hasn't been a good day.

Q500985.title: Fun on the ice
Q500985.story: Down in the valley, tiny figures skate, play and fall on the frozen ponds. Bruegel fills the cold scene with everyday life.

Q500985.title: A sign about to fall
Q500985.story: Outside the inn on the left, the signboard hangs loose from one hook. It is one of many small, real details that make this winter feel lived in.

Q533619.title: Over 100 sayings
Q533619.story: This village is packed with more than 100 Dutch proverbs acted out literally, like a man banging his head against a wall. It works like a giant visual puzzle.

Q533619.title: The blue cloak
Q533619.story: A woman drapes a blue cloak over her husband. In old Dutch, this meant she was deceiving him, and the painting was sometimes called The Blue Cloak.

Q1212937.title: The hidden skull
Q1212937.story: The strange smear across the floor is a stretched skull. Stand to the side of the painting and look along it, and the skull snaps into shape, a reminder of death amid all this wealth.

Q1212937.title: A broken string
Q1212937.story: On the lower shelf lies a lute with one broken string, often read as a sign of disharmony, at a time when Europe was splitting over religion.

Q1212937.title: A half-hidden cross
Q1212937.story: In the very top left corner, a small crucifix peeks out from behind the green curtain.

Q930137.title: A painting nobody can explain
Q930137.story: Lightning splits the sky over a city while a soldier and a mother with a baby ignore each other. Scholars have offered dozens of explanations, and none has won.

Q930137.title: A changed mind
Q930137.story: X-rays show that Giorgione first painted a woman bathing where the soldier now stands, then changed his mind.

Q727875.title: The maids in the background
Q727875.story: In the room behind, two maids search a large chest, likely for clothes. Chests like this were part of a bride's dowry, so many think the painting celebrates a marriage.

Q563727.title: The child and the lamb
Q563727.story: The baby Jesus grabs a lamb, a symbol of his future sacrifice, while his mother gently tries to hold him back. Leonardo worked on this painting for years and never quite finished it.

Q208758.title: The painter paints himself
Q208758.story: On the left, Velázquez stands at a huge canvas, brush in hand, looking straight out at us. The red cross on his chest was added later, after he was made a knight.

Q208758.title: The king and queen in the mirror
Q208758.story: On the back wall, a small mirror reflects the king and queen of Spain. They seem to stand exactly where you are, so you become part of the scene.

Q208758.title: The little princess
Q208758.story: At the centre stands the five-year-old Princess Margaret Theresa, attended by her maids of honour, the 'meninas' who give the painting its name.

Q208758.title: The man in the doorway
Q208758.story: At the back, a court official pauses on the stairs in a bright doorway, adding even more depth to this puzzle of looking and being looked at.

Q1133420.title: Handing over the key
Q1133420.story: The defeated Dutch commander hands the keys of Breda to the Spanish general, who kindly stops him from kneeling. Velázquez turned a surrender into a moment of respect.

Q1133420.title: A forest of lances
Q1133420.story: The tall, straight lances of the Spanish army give the painting its nickname in Spain, Las Lanzas.

Q275349.title: A blurry reflection
Q275349.story: Cupid holds a mirror for Venus, but her reflected face is soft and blurred, so we never quite see who she is.

Q275349.title: Attacked in protest
Q275349.story: In 1914, the campaigner Mary Richardson slashed this painting with a meat cleaver at the National Gallery in London, protesting the arrest of the suffragette leader Emmeline Pankhurst. It was carefully repaired.

Q2727560.title: A signature in red
Q2727560.story: This is the only painting Caravaggio ever signed, and he wrote his name in the red blood flowing on the floor.

Q2653851.title: A struggle on the diagonal
Q2653851.story: Straining men heave the cross upward along a sharp diagonal line. Rubens fills the scene with muscle and movement, typical of the energetic Baroque style.

Q1752990.title: Reaching for the poison
Q1752990.story: Condemned to death, the philosopher Socrates reaches for the cup of hemlock while still teaching, his other hand raised toward the heavens.

Q1752990.title: Plato at the end of the bed
Q1752990.story: The old man sitting quietly at the foot of the bed is Plato, Socrates's famous student, shown deep in thought. In reality Plato was young and not present, but David included him anyway.

Q476458.title: Three brothers swear
Q476458.story: Three brothers stretch out their arms and swear to fight for Rome. Their straight, hard lines express duty and courage.

Q476458.title: The father's swords
Q476458.story: At the centre, their father holds up three swords, the point where all the arms and lines meet.

Q476458.title: The grieving women
Q476458.story: On the right, the women of the family collapse in sorrow, knowing that whatever happens, someone they love will die.

Q636537.title: The fatal letter
Q636537.story: Marat, a leader of the French Revolution, still holds a letter from Charlotte Corday, the woman who gained entry by pretending to need his help, then killed him in his bath.

Q636537.title: A painter's tribute
Q636537.story: On the wooden crate, David painted a dedication, 'To Marat, David'. The two were friends, and David turned Marat into a martyr of the Revolution.

Q604761.title: A daring blue
Q604761.story: Gainsborough dressed the boy almost entirely in shimmering blue. Many believe he was answering a rival painter who claimed blue should never dominate a picture.

Q604761.title: A famous journey
Q604761.story: When it was sold to an American collector in 1921, crowds came to say goodbye before it left London. In 2022 it returned to London on loan for the first time in about a hundred years.

Q2629559.title: A flying slipper
Q2629559.story: As the young woman swings high, one pink slipper flies off her foot into the air, the most famous detail of this playful painting.

Q2629559.title: The hidden admirer
Q2629559.story: Down in the bushes, a young man reaches up, clearly enjoying the view. He is in on the secret, while the older man pushing the swing seems not to notice.

Q2629559.title: Keep it quiet
Q2629559.story: A statue of Cupid holds a finger to his lips, as if asking us to keep this flirtation a secret.

Q1167796.title: A bird in a jar
Q1167796.story: A travelling scientist pumps the air out of a glass jar holding a cockatoo, showing that living things need air. Will he let the air back in before it's too late?

Q1167796.title: Too scary to watch
Q1167796.story: Two young girls are upset; one covers her eyes while her father gently explains. Each person reacts differently to the science.

Q2317837.title: A demon on her chest
Q2317837.story: A grinning demon squats on the sleeping woman, a way of picturing the heavy, frightening feeling of a bad dream.

Q2317837.title: The nightmare horse
Q2317837.story: A ghostly horse with blank eyes pushes through the curtain, a visual play on the word 'nightmare'. The painting caused a sensation in 1782.

Q29530.title: Liberty herself
Q29530.story: A woman representing Liberty leads the people over the barricade, raising the red, white and blue flag of France. She is often said to have helped inspire the Statue of Liberty.

Q29530.title: The boy with pistols
Q29530.story: A young boy charges forward waving two pistols. He is often linked to Gavroche, the street boy in Victor Hugo's novel Les Misérables, written decades later.

Q29530.title: The man in the top hat
Q29530.story: The man in the top hat holding a gun has sometimes been seen as a self-portrait of Delacroix, though most experts doubt it.

Q29530.title: Notre-Dame in the smoke
Q29530.story: Far in the background, the towers of Notre-Dame Cathedral rise through the smoke, telling us this is Paris, during the July Revolution of 1830.

Q212616.title: A tiny ship on the horizon
Q212616.story: Look at the far horizon: a speck of a ship. The survivors wave desperately, hoping to be seen. The real rescue ship did finally save them.

Q212616.title: Waving for rescue
Q212616.story: At the top of the pile of bodies, a man waves a cloth toward the horizon, the moment hope returns.

Q212616.title: A real disaster
Q212616.story: In 1816 the French ship Medusa ran aground and about 150 people were left on a raft; only a handful survived. Géricault interviewed survivors and even built a model of the raft.

Q1091086.title: Arms raised
Q1091086.story: The man in the white shirt throws up his arms like a figure on a cross. Look at his hand and you may see a mark like a wound.

Q1091086.title: Faceless soldiers
Q1091086.story: The firing squad stands with its back to us, faces hidden, like a machine rather than people.

Q1091086.title: The lantern's light
Q1091086.story: A big lantern on the ground lights the victims, making them the bright centre of this dark night in 1808, when Napoleon's troops executed Spanish citizens.

Q1150997.title: Painted on his own walls
Q1150997.story: Goya painted this on a wall of his house, one of his so-called Black Paintings, never meant for the public. It was moved onto canvas after his death.

Q1231009.title: Napoleon crowns Josephine
Q1231009.story: David chose not to show Napoleon crowning himself, but the gentler moment when he crowned his wife Josephine.

Q1231009.title: A guest who wasn't there
Q1231009.story: Napoleon's mother appears in the place of honour in the gallery, yet she did not actually attend. Napoleon asked David to include her anyway.

Q1978815.title: An impossibly long back
Q1978815.story: Critics joked that this figure had a few extra vertebrae. Ingres stretched her back and arm on purpose, choosing elegance over accurate anatomy.

Q478271.title: Writing a rude letter
Q478271.story: The Cossacks are writing a mocking reply to the Ottoman Sultan, who had demanded their surrender. The scribe writes while everyone else suggests insults.

Q478271.title: A room full of laughter
Q478271.story: Repin spent years on this painting and gave each Cossack his own kind of laugh, from a quiet smile to a belly laugh.

Q152509.title: A scandal in 1863
Q152509.story: Rejected by the official Salon, this painting was shown at the Salon des Refusés, an exhibition of rejected works, where it shocked crowds. It became a landmark of modern art.

Q152509.title: The giant bather
Q152509.story: The woman in the stream behind seems far too big for her distance, one of the ways Manet broke the old rules of perspective.

Q737062.title: She stares back
Q737062.story: The woman looks straight at the viewer with calm confidence. Viewers in 1865 found that direct gaze shocking.

Q737062.title: The maid with flowers
Q737062.story: A maid brings a bouquet from an admirer. She was modelled by a woman named Laure, and recent exhibitions have brought renewed attention to her role.

Q674846.title: Clashing colours
Q674846.story: Van Gogh wrote that he wanted to express 'the terrible passions of humanity' through clashing reds and greens in this all-night café.

Q674846.title: Just after midnight
Q674846.story: The clock above the doorway shows a quarter past twelve. The billiard table casts a long shadow, while a few lonely customers sit around the edges.
